claim: Multiple genotoxic agents promoted BCL6 transactivation.
source: Multiple genotoxic agents promoted BCL6 transactivation, which was positively correlated with a weakened therapeutic efficacy and a worse clinical outcome.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: BCL6 transactivation was positively correlated with a weakened therapeutic efficacy.
source: Multiple genotoxic agents promoted BCL6 transactivation, which was positively correlated with a weakened therapeutic efficacy and a worse clinical outcome.
evidence: The abstract states this correlation, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: BCL6 transactivation was positively correlated with a worse clinical outcome.
source: Multiple genotoxic agents promoted BCL6 transactivation, which was positively correlated with a weakened therapeutic efficacy and a worse clinical outcome.
evidence: The abstract states this correlation, supported by clinical data analysis.

claim: Treatment with etoposide led to transcriptional reprogramming of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Mechanistically, we discovered that treatment with the genotoxic agent etoposide led to the transcriptional reprogramming of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, among which the interferon-α and interferon-γ responses were substantially enriched in resistant cells.
evidence: The abstract describes this mechanism, supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Interferon-α and interferon-γ responses were substantially enriched in resistant cells after etoposide treatment.
source: Mechanistically, we discovered that treatment with the genotoxic agent etoposide led to the transcriptional reprogramming of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, among which the interferon-α and interferon-γ responses were substantially enriched in resistant cells.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The activation of interferon/STAT1 axis directly upregulated BCL6 expression.
source: Our results further revealed that the activation of interferon/signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 axis directly upregulated BCL6 expression.
evidence: The abstract states this mechanism, supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing STAT1 binding to BCL6 promoter.

claim: Increased expression of BCL6 repressed the tumor suppressor PTEN.
source: The increased expression of BCL6 further repressed the tumor suppressor PTEN and consequently enabled resistant cancer cell survival.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by experimental data showing inverse correlation between BCL6 and PTEN expression.

claim: BCL6-mediated repression of PTEN enabled resistant cancer cell survival.
source: The increased expression of BCL6 further repressed the tumor suppressor PTEN and consequently enabled resistant cancer cell survival.
evidence: The abstract states this causal relationship, supported by functional assays.

claim: Targeted inhibition of BCL6 enhanced etoposide-triggered DNA damage in vitro.
source: Accordingly, targeted inhibition of BCL6 remarkably enhanced etoposide-triggered DNA damage and apoptosis both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by comet assays and p-H2AX expression data.

claim: Targeted inhibition of BCL6 enhanced etoposide-triggered apoptosis in vitro.
source: Accordingly, targeted inhibition of BCL6 remarkably enhanced etoposide-triggered DNA damage and apoptosis both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by flow cytometry data showing increased apoptotic cells.

claim: Targeted inhibition of BCL6 enhanced etoposide-triggered DNA damage in vivo.
source: Accordingly, targeted inhibition of BCL6 remarkably enhanced etoposide-triggered DNA damage and apoptosis both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by xenograft mouse model data.

claim: Targeted inhibition of BCL6 enhanced etoposide-triggered apoptosis in vivo.
source: Accordingly, targeted inhibition of BCL6 remarkably enhanced etoposide-triggered DNA damage and apoptosis both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by xenograft mouse model data.

claim: Genome instability is the major hallmark of chronic proliferating tumors.
source: Genome instability is the major hallmark of chronic proliferating tumors (Hanahan, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hanahan, 2022.

claim: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy introduces DNA damage lesions.
source: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy (e.g. topoisomerase II inhibitors, cisplatin, and carboplatin) that introduce DNA damage lesions, devastate genomic integrity and activate pro-apoptotic pathways, are employed as the standard first-line treatment for a wide array of solid malignancies.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of genotoxic chemotherapy.

claim: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy devastates genomic integrity.
source: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy (e.g. topoisomerase II inhibitors, cisplatin, and carboplatin) that introduce DNA damage lesions, devastate genomic integrity and activate pro-apoptotic pathways, are employed as the standard first-line treatment for a wide array of solid malignancies.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of genotoxic chemotherapy.

claim: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy activates pro-apoptotic pathways.
source: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy (e.g. topoisomerase II inhibitors, cisplatin, and carboplatin) that introduce DNA damage lesions, devastate genomic integrity and activate pro-apoptotic pathways, are employed as the standard first-line treatment for a wide array of solid malignancies.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of genotoxic chemotherapy.

claim: Genotoxic chemotherapy is employed as the standard first-line treatment for a wide array of solid malignancies.
source: Conventional genotoxic chemotherapy (e.g. topoisomerase II inhibitors, cisplatin, and carboplatin) that introduce DNA damage lesions, devastate genomic integrity and activate pro-apoptotic pathways, are employed as the standard first-line treatment for a wide array of solid malignancies.
evidence: This is established clinical practice.

claim: Intrinsic resistance or rapid adaptive resistance in cancer cells is a major hurdle hampering the clinical efficacy of genotoxic agents.
source: Despite initial therapeutic success, intrinsic resistance or rapid adaptive resistance in cancer cells is a major hurdle, hampering the clinical efficacy of these agents (Liang et al., 2019; Stebbing et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2019 and Stebbing et al., 2018.

claim: Chemoresistance occurs due to an increased DNA damage repair capacity.
source: Chemoresistance occurs due to complex reasons, such as an increased DNA damage repair capacity, activation of pro-survival pathways, and defects in caspase activity (Bernard et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Chemoresistance occurs due to activation of pro-survival pathways.
source: Chemoresistance occurs due to complex reasons, such as an increased DNA damage repair capacity, activation of pro-survival pathways, and defects in caspase activity (Bernard et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Chemoresistance occurs due to defects in caspase activity.
source: Chemoresistance occurs due to complex reasons, such as an increased DNA damage repair capacity, activation of pro-survival pathways, and defects in caspase activity (Bernard et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2019; Poth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: ABCA1 is a predictive marker in tumor tolerance to genotoxic agents.
source: While several signaling effectors have been identified as predictive markers, such as ABCA1 (Koh et al., 2019) and MAST1 (Jin et al., 2018), in tumor tolerance to genotoxic agents, the majority of these studies lacked either an evaluation of the clinical correlation or an explanation for how these effectors mediate pro-survival signals in the context of genotoxic stress.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Koh et al., 2019.

claim: MAST1 is a predictive marker in tumor tolerance to genotoxic agents.
source: While several signaling effectors have been identified as predictive markers, such as ABCA1 (Koh et al., 2019) and MAST1 (Jin et al., 2018), in tumor tolerance to genotoxic agents, the majority of these studies lacked either an evaluation of the clinical correlation or an explanation for how these effectors mediate pro-survival signals in the context of genotoxic stress.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2018.

claim: BCL6 has emerged as a critical therapeutic target in diffuse large B-cell lymphomas.
source: The transcriptional repressor BCL6 has emerged as a critical therapeutic target in diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (Parekh et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parekh et al., 2008.

claim: BCL6 plays an oncogenic role in several human hematopoietic malignancies and solid tumors.
source: Increasing evidences indicate that BCL6 plays an oncogenic role in several human hematopoietic malignancies and solid tumors (Cardenas et al., 2017; Deb et al., 2017; Kawabata et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cardenas et al., 2017; Deb et al., 2017; Kawabata et al., 2021.

claim: BCL6 binds and represses different target genes to drive tumorigenesis in a cell context-dependent manner.
source: BCL6 binds and represses different target genes to drive tumorigenesis in a cell context-dependent manner (Ci et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ci et al., 2009.

claim: Constitutive expression of BCL6 sustains the lymphoma phenotype through transcriptional repression of the DNA damage sensor ATR.
source: The constitutive expression of BCL6 sustains the lymphoma phenotype and promotes glioblastoma through transcriptional repression of the DNA damage sensor ATR (Ranuncolo et al., 2007) and the p53 pathway (Xu et al., 2017), respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ranuncolo et al., 2007.

claim: Constitutive expression of BCL6 promotes glioblastoma through transcriptional repression of the p53 pathway.
source: The constitutive expression of BCL6 sustains the lymphoma phenotype and promotes glioblastoma through transcriptional repression of the DNA damage sensor ATR (Ranuncolo et al., 2007) and the p53 pathway (Xu et al., 2017), respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2017.

claim: The BCL6 locus is predominantly amplified in primary breast cancer according to TCGA data.
source: According to data derived from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), the BCL6 locus is also predominantly amplified in primary breast cancer and is correlated with a worse prognosis (Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2015 and references TCGA data.

claim: BCL6 amplification in primary breast cancer is correlated with a worse prognosis.
source: According to data derived from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), the BCL6 locus is also predominantly amplified in primary breast cancer and is correlated with a worse prognosis (Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2015.

claim: Small molecular inhibitors that target the interaction between BCL6 and its co-repressors effectively restored BCL6 target gene expression and impeded tumor growth.
source: In recent years, small molecular inhibitors that target the interaction between BCL6 and its co-repressors or that trigger BCL6 degradation effectively restored BCL6 target gene expression and impeded tumor growth (Cardenas et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2018; Słabicki et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cardenas et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2018; Słabicki et al., 2020.

claim: Small molecular inhibitors that trigger BCL6 degradation effectively restored BCL6 target gene expression and impeded tumor growth.
source: In recent years, small molecular inhibitors that target the interaction between BCL6 and its co-repressors or that trigger BCL6 degradation effectively restored BCL6 target gene expression and impeded tumor growth (Cardenas et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2018; Słabicki et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cardenas et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2018; Słabicki et al., 2020.

claim: BCL6 sustains the proliferative and stress-tolerant phenotype of germinal center B cells.
source: The properties of BCL6 as a therapeutic target originate from its normal function in sustaining the proliferative and the phenotype of stress-tolerant germinal center B cells (Liu et al., 2021; Phan et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2021; Phan et al., 2007.

claim: BCL6 allows B cells to evade ATR-mediated checkpoints by repressing cell cycle checkpoint genes and DNA damage sensing genes.
source: BCL6 allows B cells to evade ATR-mediated checkpoints and tolerate exogenous DNA damage by repressing the cell cycle checkpoint genes CDKN1A, CDKN1B, and CDKN2B, and the DNA damage sensing genes TP53, CHEK1, and ATR (Basso et al., 2010; Cardenas et al., 2017; Phan et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Basso et al., 2010; Cardenas et al., 2017; Phan et al., 2005.

claim: BCL6 is phosphorylated by ATM kinase and degraded through the ubiquitin proteasome system when genotoxic stress accumulates.
source: When genotoxic stress is accumulated to some extent, BCL6 is phosphorylated by the DNA damage sensor ATM kinase and degraded through the ubiquitin proteasome system, whereby the germinal center reaction is terminated (Phan et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Phan et al., 2007.

claim: The critical functions exerted by BCL6 during normal B cell development could be hijacked by malignant transformation, leading to lymphoma.
source: The critical functions exerted by BCL6 during normal B cell development could be hijacked by malignant transformation, thereby leading to lymphoma (Basso and Dalla-Favera, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Basso and Dalla-Favera, 2012.

claim: BCL6 can be activated by heat shock factor 1 to tolerate heat stress.
source: In more detail, BCL6 can be activated by heat shock factor 1 to tolerate heat stress (Fernando et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fernando et al., 2019.

claim: Aberrant expression of BCL6 can be provoked in leukemia cells in response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib.
source: The aberrant expression of BCL6 can be provoked in leukemia cells in response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (Duy et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Duy et al., 2011.

claim: Increased expression of BCL6 largely contributes to the resistance of KRAS-mutant lung cancer to clinical BET inhibitors.
source: Our recent work additionally revealed that an increased expression of BCL6 largely contributes to the resistance of KRAS-mutant lung cancer to clinical BET inhibitors (Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2021.

claim: Some cell lines displayed apparent resistance to etoposide at doses up to 30 μM.
source: Some cell lines displayed apparent resistance to etoposide at doses up to 30 μM (Figure 1A) or to doxorubicin at doses up to 0.6 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), while the remaining cell lines showed a gradient of sensitivity to them.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some cell lines displayed apparent resistance to doxorubicin at doses up to 0.6 μM.
source: Some cell lines displayed apparent resistance to etoposide at doses up to 30 μM (Figure 1A) or to doxorubicin at doses up to 0.6 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), while the remaining cell lines showed a gradient of sensitivity to them.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The concentrations of 30 μM etoposide and 0.6 μM doxorubicin are the highest achievable concentration in the plasma of patients.
source: The concentrations of 30 μM and 0.6 μM were chosen to define the resistance of multiple cancer cell lines to etoposide and doxorubicin, respectively, as these are the highest achievable concentration in the plasma of patients, which are likely to be clinically relevant (Kaul et al., 1995; Palle et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kaul et al., 1995; Palle et al., 2006.

claim: Etoposide treatment triggered a remarkable increase in BCL6 expression in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 and H661 cells, but not in etoposide-sensitive PC9 cells.
source: By analyzing the significantly differentially expressed genes, we found that etoposide treatment triggered a remarkable increase in BCL6 expression in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 and H661 cells, but not in etoposide-sensitive PC9 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The BCL6 transcriptional program was dramatically affected by etoposide in treated Capan-2 and H661 cells, but not in treated PC9 cells.
source: Our data revealed that the BCL6 transcriptional program was dramatically affected by etoposide in treated Capan-2 and H661 cells, but not in treated PC9 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BCL6 upregulation was observed in acquired resistance process after chemotherapy.
source: Therefore, we analyzed published microarray data (Januchowski et al., 2014; Moitra et al., 2012), and found that BCL6 upregulation was also observed in acquired resistance process (Figure 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of published microarray data cited as Januchowski et al., 2014; Moitra et al., 2012.

claim: BCL6 was upregulated in response to the majority of frontline genotoxic agents.
source: The results showed that BCL6 was upregulated in response to the majority of these clinical agents (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A high expression of BCL6 was associated with a poor progression-free survival in patients who received cisplatin, taxol, or both drugs.
source: In addition, a high expression of BCL6 was associated with a poor progression-free survival in patients who received cisplatin, taxol, or both drugs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This statement is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: BCL6 protein abundance was dramatically and preferentially induced by etoposide in resistant cells compared to that in sensitive cells.
source: In agreement with the BCL6 transcription pattern observed in Figure 1C, BCL6 protein abundance was dramatically and preferentially induced by etoposide in resistant cells compared to that in sensitive cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased BCL6 protein levels were closely associated with increased etoposide IC50 values.
source: Notably, increased BCL6 protein levels were closely associated with increased etoposide IC50 values (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells with higher BCL6 protein levels were prone to be more tolerant to etoposide (R2=0.61, p<0.0001).
source: Specifically, cells with higher BCL6 protein levels were prone to be more tolerant to etoposide (R2=0.61, p<0.0001; Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BCL6 protein expression could be time-dependently provoked by a long-term exposure of resistant cells to etoposide.
source: A more detailed observation demonstrated that BCL6 protein expression could also be time-dependently provoked by a long-term exposure of resistant cells to etoposide (Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Etoposide impeded the growth of PANC28 and HCT116 xenografts at a dose of 10 mg/kg/day.
source: Our results showed that etoposide impeded the growth at a dose of 10 mg/kg/day (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This statement is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: BCL6 protein levels in PANC28 and HCT116 xenografts were dramatically increased by etoposide.
source: When noted, the BCL6 protein levels in the PANC28 and HCT116 xenografts were dramatically increased by etoposide (Figure 2D), which was consistent with our in vitro observations.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data from xenografts shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BCL6 genetic knockdown dramatically attenuated the clonogenic growth of Capan-2 and HCT116 cells in the presence of etoposide.
source: Next, to examine whether BCL6 transactivation affects drug efficacy in resistant cells, we targeted BCL6 using two different small interfering RNAs and found that BCL6 genetic knockdown dramatically attenuated the clonogenic growth of Capan-2 and HCT116 cells in the presence of etoposide (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: Inducible knockdown of BCL6 potentiated the killing effects of etoposide.
source: In line with these results, inducible knockdown of BCL6 potentiated the killing effects of etoposide (Figure 2G).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: BCL6 overexpression increased the etoposide IC50 by up to 17-fold in H522 cells.
source: As expected, our results showed that BCL6 overexpression increased the etoposide IC50 by up to 17-fold (Figure 2H).
evidence: This statement is supported by SRB assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Differentially expressed genes related to inflammatory and immune responses were enriched in resistant Capan-2 and H661 cells, but not in sensitive PC9 cells.
source: Intriguingly, the differentially genes related to inflammatory and immune responses were enriched in resistant Capan-2 and H661 cells, but not in sensitive PC9 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), raising the possibility that pro-inflammatory factors may play a causal role in conferring chemoresistance.
evidence: This statement is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genes associated with interferon-alpha response, inflammatory response, and interferon-gamma response were significantly upregulated in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis further demonstrated a significant upregulation of genes associated with interferon-alpha (IFN-α) response, inflammatory response, and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) response in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 cells (Figure 3A–C) and H661 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Genes associated with interferon-alpha response, inflammatory response, and interferon-gamma response were significantly upregulated in etoposide-resistant H661 cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis further demonstrated a significant upregulation of genes associated with interferon-alpha (IFN-α) response, inflammatory response, and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) response in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 cells (Figure 3A–C) and H661 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Etoposide exposure resulted in an evident upregulation of IFN-α transcription in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 and PANC28 cells, but not in etoposide-sensitive H522, PC9, and PANC-1 cells.
source: Our results showed that etoposide exposure resulted in an evident upregulation of IFN-α (Figure 3F) and IFN-γ transcription (Figure 3G) in etoposide-resistant Capan-2, and PANC28 cells, but not in etoposide-sensitive H522, PC9, and PANC-1 cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Etoposide exposure resulted in an evident upregulation of IFN-γ transcription in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 and PANC28 cells, but not in etoposide-sensitive H522, PC9, and PANC-1 cells.
source: Our results showed that etoposide exposure resulted in an evident upregulation of IFN-α (Figure 3F) and IFN-γ transcription (Figure 3G) in etoposide-resistant Capan-2, and PANC28 cells, but not in etoposide-sensitive H522, PC9, and PANC-1 cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Etoposide treatment evoked a significant increase in IFN-α contents in resistant cells.
source: We further examined the cellular production of IFN-α and IFN-γ in treated resistant cells using a direct enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and found that etoposide treatment evoked a significant increase in IFN-α (Figure 3H) and IFN-γ contents (Figure 3I) in resistant cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Etoposide treatment evoked a significant increase in IFN-γ contents in resistant cells.
source: We further examined the cellular production of IFN-α and IFN-γ in treated resistant cells using a direct enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and found that etoposide treatment evoked a significant increase in IFN-α (Figure 3H) and IFN-γ contents (Figure 3I) in resistant cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Etoposide triggered a notable increase in IRF1 transcription in resistant cells.
source: We found that etoposide not only triggered a notable increase in IRF1 transcription itself, but also dramatically enhanced IFN-α- and IFN-γ-induced IRF1 expression (Figure 3J–K), indicating the potent effect of etoposide on cellular interferon responses.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J–K.

claim: Etoposide dramatically enhanced IFN-α-induced IRF1 expression.
source: We found that etoposide not only triggered a notable increase in IRF1 transcription itself, but also dramatically enhanced IFN-α- and IFN-γ-induced IRF1 expression (Figure 3J–K), indicating the potent effect of etoposide on cellular interferon responses.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Etoposide dramatically enhanced IFN-γ-induced IRF1 expression.
source: We found that etoposide not only triggered a notable increase in IRF1 transcription itself, but also dramatically enhanced IFN-α- and IFN-γ-induced IRF1 expression (Figure 3J–K), indicating the potent effect of etoposide on cellular interferon responses.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Exogenous addition of IFN-α protected sensitive cells from etoposide-induced cell death.
source: Our results showed that exogenous addition of IFN-α and IFN-γ protected sensitive cells from etoposide-induced cell death (Figure 3L–M).
evidence: This statement is supported by SRB assay data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Exogenous addition of IFN-γ protected sensitive cells from etoposide-induced cell death.
source: Our results showed that exogenous addition of IFN-α and IFN-γ protected sensitive cells from etoposide-induced cell death (Figure 3L–M).
evidence: This statement is supported by SRB assay data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: siRNA knockdown of IFNAR1 led to an enhanced sensitivity of resistant cells to etoposide.
source: In contrast, siRNA knockdown of the IFN-α receptor IFNAR1 led to an enhanced sensitivity of resistant cells to etoposide, as indicated by impaired clonogenic growth (Figure 3N) and decreased IC50 values of etoposide (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 3N and IC50 data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Antibodies against IFN-γ increased the killing ability of etoposide towards resistant cells.
source: In line with these observations, antibodies against IFN-γ increased the killing ability of etoposide towards resistant cells (Figure 3O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 3O and IC50 data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Etoposide treatment promoted STAT1 abundance and activation in etoposide-resistant Capan-2, PANC28, and H838 cells, but not in sensitive H522, PC9, and PANC-1 cells.
source: Following this direction, we examined STAT1 expression in treated cells and found that etoposide treatment promoted STAT1 abundance and activation in etoposide-resistant Capan-2, PANC28, and H838 cells, but not in sensitive H522, PC9, and PANC-1 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genetic knockdown of STAT1 synergized with genotoxic agents to inhibit the clonogenic growth of resistant cells.
source: Furthermore, genetic knockdown of STAT1 synergized with genotoxic agents to inhibit the clonogenic growth of resistant cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IFN-α significantly evoked an increase in BCL6 mRNA expression in resistant cells.
source: Given the regulation of IFN-stimulated gene expression specifically through the classical Janus kinase/STAT1 signaling, we first incubated resistant cells with recombinant IFN-α and IFN-γ and found that they significantly evoked a simultaneous increase in BCL6 mRNA expression (Figure 4C–D), and STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression (Figure 4E–F), implying that these two factors might be functionally linked.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IFN-γ significantly evoked an increase in BCL6 mRNA expression in resistant cells.
source: Given the regulation of IFN-stimulated gene expression specifically through the classical Janus kinase/STAT1 signaling, we first incubated resistant cells with recombinant IFN-α and IFN-γ and found that they significantly evoked a simultaneous increase in BCL6 mRNA expression (Figure 4C–D), and STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression (Figure 4E–F), implying that these two factors might be functionally linked.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IFN-α significantly evoked an increase in STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression in resistant cells.
source: Given the regulation of IFN-stimulated gene expression specifically through the classical Janus kinase/STAT1 signaling, we first incubated resistant cells with recombinant IFN-α and IFN-γ and found that they significantly evoked a simultaneous increase in BCL6 mRNA expression (Figure 4C–D), and STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression (Figure 4E–F), implying that these two factors might be functionally linked.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: IFN-γ significantly evoked an increase in STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression in resistant cells.
source: Given the regulation of IFN-stimulated gene expression specifically through the classical Janus kinase/STAT1 signaling, we first incubated resistant cells with recombinant IFN-α and IFN-γ and found that they significantly evoked a simultaneous increase in BCL6 mRNA expression (Figure 4C–D), and STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression (Figure 4E–F), implying that these two factors might be functionally linked.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Etoposide-mediated BCL6 transactivation could be further enhanced in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 cells by the addition of IFN-α or IFN-γ.
source: Our results showed that etoposide-mediated BCL6 transactivation could be further enhanced in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 cells (Figure 4G–H) and PANC28 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) by the addition of IFN-α or IFN-γ.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4G–H.

claim: Etoposide-mediated BCL6 transactivation could be further enhanced in etoposide-resistant PANC28 cells by the addition of IFN-α or IFN-γ.
source: Our results showed that etoposide-mediated BCL6 transactivation could be further enhanced in etoposide-resistant Capan-2 cells (Figure 4G–H) and PANC28 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) by the addition of IFN-α or IFN-γ.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Etoposide induced STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression in resistant cells, and these effects could be potentiated by IFN-α addition.
source: Moreover, etoposide induced STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression in resistant cells, whereas these effects could be potentiated by IFN-α (Figure 4I) or IFN-γ addition (Figure 4J), implying that etoposide-induced type 1 and type 2 interferon responses are required for STAT1 and BCL6 activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Etoposide induced STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression in resistant cells, and these effects could be potentiated by IFN-γ addition.
source: Moreover, etoposide induced STAT1 and BCL6 protein expression in resistant cells, whereas these effects could be potentiated by IFN-α (Figure 4I) or IFN-γ addition (Figure 4J), implying that etoposide-induced type 1 and type 2 interferon responses are required for STAT1 and BCL6 activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: An increased expression of BCL6 by etoposide was apparently suppressed by STAT1 genetic silencing.
source: Importantly, an increased expression of BCL6 by etoposide was apparently suppressed by STAT1 genetic silencing (Figure 4K).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: STAT1 knockdown led to a marked decrease in BCL6 protein expression.
source: To elucidate the regulatory link of STAT1 on BCL6, we silenced STAT1 and found that STAT1 knockdown led to a marked decrease in BCL6 protein expression (Figure 4L), while STAT1 overexpression apparently increased BCL6 protein abundance (Figure 4M), implying that STAT1 may be upstream of BCL6.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: STAT1 overexpression apparently increased BCL6 protein abundance.
source: To elucidate the regulatory link of STAT1 on BCL6, we silenced STAT1 and found that STAT1 knockdown led to a marked decrease in BCL6 protein expression (Figure 4L), while STAT1 overexpression apparently increased BCL6 protein abundance (Figure 4M), implying that STAT1 may be upstream of BCL6.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: STAT1 interference resulted in a decreased BCL6 reporter activity.
source: To elucidate whether STAT1 is a direct regulator of BCL6, we constructed a whole BCL6 promoter luciferase reporter and found that STAT1 interference resulted in a decreased BCL6 reporter activity (Figure 4N).
evidence: This statement is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: STAT1 is recruited to three putative binding regions of the BCL6 locus.
source: Our chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with qPCR analysis further revealed the recruitment of STAT1 to three putative binding regions of the BCL6 locus (Figure 4O).
evidence: This statement is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: PTEN was enriched in BCL6 promoter binding peaks in primary germinal center B cells.
source: Considering two lines of evidences showing that: (1) phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN), a lipid phosphatase that antagonizes the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase pathway, was enriched in BCL6 promoter binding peaks in primary germinal center B cells (Ci et al., 2009), and that (2) BCL6 directly binds to the promoter locus of PTEN in patient-derived acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Geng et al., 2015), we hypothesized that an increase in BCL6 expression by genotoxic stress might inhibit PTEN and subsequently promote cell survival.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ci et al., 2009.

claim: BCL6 directly binds to the promoter locus of PTEN in patient-derived acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: Considering two lines of evidences showing that: (1) phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN), a lipid phosphatase that antagonizes the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase pathway, was enriched in BCL6 promoter binding peaks in primary germinal center B cells (Ci et al., 2009), and that (2) BCL6 directly binds to the promoter locus of PTEN in patient-derived acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Geng et al., 2015), we hypothesized that an increase in BCL6 expression by genotoxic stress might inhibit PTEN and subsequently promote cell survival.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2015.

claim: There was an evident decrease in PTEN expression in Capan-2 and H661 cells exposed to etoposide.
source: To this end, we performed transcriptome analysis and found an evident decrease in PTEN expression in Capan-2 and H661 cells exposed to etoposide (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PTEN deletion was mutually exclusive with BCL6 amplification according to TCGA data.
source: The analysis of datasets from TCGA further revealed that PTEN deletion was mutually exclusive with BCL6 amplification (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The upregulation of BCL6 was accompanied by a decreased expression of PTEN at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Furthermore, our qPCR (Figure 5C) and immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5D) showed that the upregulation of BCL6 was accompanied by a decreased expression of PTEN at both the mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: BCL6 overexpression led to a significant decrease in PTEN.
source: We additionally overexpressed BCL6 and observed a significant decrease in PTEN (Figure 5E).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Doxycycline-inducible knockdown of BCL6 increased PTEN expression.
source: In contrast, doxycycline-inducible knockdown of BCL6 increased PTEN expression (Figure 5F).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Etoposide treatment significantly increased the occupancy of BCL6 at the promoter region of PTEN.
source: Our ChIP-qPCR data further revealed that etoposide treatment significantly increased the occupancy of BCL6 at the promoter region of PTEN (Figure 5G).
evidence: This statement is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Phosphorylation of mTOR (S2448), S6K (T389), and S6 (S235/S236) was strikingly increased in etoposide-treated resistant cells.
source: Our immunoblotting results showed that phosphorylation of mTOR (S2448), S6K (T389), and S6 (S235/S236) was strikingly increased, along with an aberrant BCL6 expression in etoposide-treated resistant cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: PTEN overexpression enhanced the antitumor effects of etoposide in resistant cells.
source: Notably, overexpression of PTEN enhanced the antitumor effects of etoposide in resistant cells (Figure 5J), and in contrast, PTEN deficiency significantly decreased the cytotoxicity elicited by etoposide in sensitive cells (Figure 5K).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: PTEN deficiency significantly decreased the cytotoxicity elicited by etoposide in sensitive cells.
source: Notably, overexpression of PTEN enhanced the antitumor effects of etoposide in resistant cells (Figure 5J), and in contrast, PTEN deficiency significantly decreased the cytotoxicity elicited by etoposide in sensitive cells (Figure 5K).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Multiple resistant cell lines became vulnerable to etoposide in the presence of BI3802 or compound 7.
source: Our results showed that multiple resistant cell lines became vulnerable to etoposide in the presence of BI3802 or compound 7 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by IC50 data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: BI3802 addition could shift the IC50 values of doxorubicin.
source: In addition, BI3802 addition could shift the IC50 values of doxorubicin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by IC50 data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of combination index values at 50, 75, and 90% of the effective dose of etoposide plus BI3802 or etoposide plus compound 7 in five resistant cell lines were all lower than one.
source: Moreover, combination index values (CIs) were further employed to indicate drug synergy, and our results showed that the majority of CIs at 50, 75, and 90% of the effective dose of each drug pair (etoposide plus BI3802, or etoposide plus compound 7) in five resistant cell lines were all lower than one (Figure 6B), displaying a synergistic action of etoposide and BCL6-targeted therapy.
evidence: This statement is supported by combination index data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The combination of etoposide and BI3802 led to a robust growth inhibition of cultured colonies.
source: We further assessed the combined effects of etoposide and the BCL6 inhibitor BI3802 in a long-term colony-formation assay. Our results showed that the combination of etoposide and BI3802 led to a robust growth inhibition of cultured colonies (Figure 6C).
evidence: This statement is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Addition of BI3802 markedly enhanced the inhibitory effects of etoposide on soft-agar colony formation.
source: As expected, addition of BI3802 markedly enhanced the inhibitory effects of etoposide on soft-agar colony formation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This statement is supported by soft-agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The combined regimen of etoposide and BI3802 resulted in more poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase cleavage and a higher phosphorylated H2AX expression (Ser139) than single agent alone.
source: Our results showed that the combined regimen of etoposide and BI3802 resulted in more poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase cleavage and a higher phosphorylated H2AX expression (Ser139) than single agent alone (Figure 6E).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: More DNA damage occurred as indicated by a significantly higher tail moment observed in a comet assay in the combined treatment group.
source: In addition, more DNA damage occurred as indicated by a significantly higher tail moment observed in a comet assay in the combined treatment group (Figure 6F).
evidence: This statement is supported by comet assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: An increase in the number of apoptotic cells was observed in the drug pair group.
source: Consequently, an increase in the number of apoptotic cells was observed in the drug pair group (Figure 6G).
evidence: This statement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: BCL6 was upregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in HCT116 xenografts as early as 2 days after etoposide administration, and this effect was sustained during the treatment period.
source: We found that BCL6 was upregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in xenografts as early as 2 days after drug administration, and intriguingly, this effect was sustained during the treatment period (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The addition of FX1 from day 2 significantly enhanced the therapeutic potency of etoposide in HCT116 xenografts, as indicated by a decreased tumor volume and tumor weight.
source: Strikingly, the addition of FX1 from day 2 significantly enhanced the therapeutic potency of etoposide, as indicated by a decreased tumor volume and tumor weight (Figure 7A).
evidence: This statement is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Administration of 10 mg/kg etoposide and 5 mg/kg FX1 was well-tolerated in mice since the levels of blood biochemical indicators were marginally affected.
source: Administration of 10 mg/kg etoposide and 5 mg/kg FX1 was well-tolerated in mice since the levels of blood biochemical indicators were marginally affected (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by blood biochemical data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Etoposide treatment resulted in a marked increase in p-mTOR (S2448), p-P70S6K (T389), and p-S6 (S235/S236) expression levels in xenografts, whereas addition of FX1 suppressed the activation of the mTOR signaling pathway.
source: Immunoblot analysis of tumor lysates revealed a marked increase in p-mTOR (S2448), p-P70S6K (T389), and p-S6 (S235/S236) expression levels in etoposide-treated xenografts, whereas addition of FX1 suppressed the activation of the mTOR signaling pathway (Figure 7B).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Immunohistochemistry analysis showed an increase in p-H2AX (S139) expression and weaker Ki-67 signals in the xenografts from the drug pair group.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis additionally showed an increase in p-H2AX (S139) expression and weaker Ki-67 signals in the xenografts from the drug pair group (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a fundamental role of BCL6-targeted therapy in sensitizing etoposide in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BCL6 genetic silencing markedly sensitized etoposide in PANC28 xenograft mice.
source: To further confirm the sensitizing action of BCL6 blockade to etoposide, we additionally set up a tumor xenograft mouse model using PANC28 cells that are more resistant of etoposide treatment than HCT116 cells. Our results consistently showed that BCL6 genetic silencing markedly sensitized etoposide in mice. The combination of etoposide and BCL6 knockdown significantly impeded PANC28 tumor growth compared to etoposide treatment alone group (Figure 7C).
evidence: This statement is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The combination of etoposide and FX1 significantly suppressed tumor weight and tumor volume in LACPDX compared with single agent alone.
source: To evaluate the antitumor activity of FX1 + etoposide in a more clinically relevant mouse model, we established a patient-derived xenograft model of lung adenocarcinoma harboring a G12V mutation in KRAS (LACPDX). Our results showed that the combination of etoposide and FX1 significantly suppressed tumor weight and tumor volume compared with single agent alone (Figure 7D), without causing systemic toxicity in mice ( Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Addition of FX1 markedly decreased p-S6 (S235/S236) expression and increased p-H2AX (S139) expression in LACPDX.
source: In agreement, addition of FX1 markedly decreased p-S6 (S235/S236) expression and increased p-H2AX (S139) expression in LACPDX (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BCL6 functions as a central factor in mediating chemoresistance through the interferon/STAT1 pathway serving as an upstream regulator of BCL6.
source: Our current findings support the notion that BCL6 functions as a central factor in mediating chemoresistance: (1) the interferon/STAT1 pathway serves as an upstream regulator of BCL6, (2) the tumor suppressor PTEN is identified as a functional target of BCL6, (3) the activation of BCL6 signaling leads to a sustained pro-survival phenotype, whereas blocking it enhances the therapeutic efficacy of genotoxic agents.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: The tumor suppressor PTEN is identified as a functional target of BCL6.
source: Our current findings support the notion that BCL6 functions as a central factor in mediating chemoresistance: (1) the interferon/STAT1 pathway serves as an upstream regulator of BCL6, (2) the tumor suppressor PTEN is identified as a functional target of BCL6, (3) the activation of BCL6 signaling leads to a sustained pro-survival phenotype, whereas blocking it enhances the therapeutic efficacy of genotoxic agents.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: The activation of BCL6 signaling leads to a sustained pro-survival phenotype.
source: Our current findings support the notion that BCL6 functions as a central factor in mediating chemoresistance: (1) the interferon/STAT1 pathway serves as an upstream regulator of BCL6, (2) the tumor suppressor PTEN is identified as a functional target of BCL6, (3) the activation of BCL6 signaling leads to a sustained pro-survival phenotype, whereas blocking it enhances the therapeutic efficacy of genotoxic agents.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking BCL6 signaling enhances the therapeutic efficacy of genotoxic agents.
source: Our current findings support the notion that BCL6 functions as a central factor in mediating chemoresistance: (1) the interferon/STAT1 pathway serves as an upstream regulator of BCL6, (2) the tumor suppressor PTEN is identified as a functional target of BCL6, (3) the activation of BCL6 signaling leads to a sustained pro-survival phenotype, whereas blocking it enhances the therapeutic efficacy of genotoxic agents.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: BCL6 acts as a gatekeeper to protect germinal center B cells from undergoing somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination against DNA damage.
source: BCL6 acts as a gatekeeper to protect germinal center B cells from undergoing somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination against DNA damage (Duy et al., 2010; Polo et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Duy et al., 2010; Polo et al., 2008.

claim: Consistent DNA damage triggers an inflammatory cytokine secretory phenotype in cultured cells.
source: Recent work has revealed that consistent DNA damage triggers an inflammatory cytokine secretory phenotype in cultured cells (Rodier et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rodier et al., 2009.

claim: IRF1 is a key transcription factor that regulates cell proliferation and immune responses.
source: Interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1), a key transcription factor that regulates cell proliferation and immune responses, is an inducible gene of type I and type II interferon (Dery et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dery et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: IRF1 is an inducible gene of type I and type II interferon.
source: Interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1), a key transcription factor that regulates cell proliferation and immune responses, is an inducible gene of type I and type II interferon (Dery et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dery et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: IFNs produce pro-survival effects and mediate non-immune resistance to chemotherapy primarily through the transcriptional factor STAT1.
source: Accumulating evidences show that IFNs produce pro-survival effects and mediate non-immune resistance to chemotherapy primarily through the transcriptional factor STAT1 (Minn, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Minn, 2015.

claim: Activated STAT1 drives an interferon-related gene signature for DNA damage tolerance.
source: Activated STAT1 drives an interferon-related gene signature for DNA damage tolerance (Minn, 2015), which prompted us to hypothesize that the interferon/STAT1 axis might regulate BCL6 expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Minn, 2015.

claim: PTEN acts as a tumor suppressor and hampers the activation of the proto-oncogenic mTOR pathway.
source: It is well-known that PTEN acts as a tumor suppressor and hampers the activation of the proto-oncogenic mTOR pathway (Mukherjee et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mukherjee et al., 2021.

claim: BI3802 was reported as a BCL6 degrader.
source: We suppressed BCL6's function using two BCL6 pharmacological inhibitors, BI3802 and compound 7. BI3802 was reported as a BCL6 degrader (Słabicki et al., 2020), while compound 7 targeted the BCL6 BTB/POZ domain and prevented its partner binding (Kamada et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Słabicki et al., 2020.

claim: Compound 7 targeted the BCL6 BTB/POZ domain and prevented its partner binding.
source: We suppressed BCL6's function using two BCL6 pharmacological inhibitors, BI3802 and compound 7. BI3802 was reported as a BCL6 degrader (Słabicki et al., 2020), while compound 7 targeted the BCL6 BTB/POZ domain and prevented its partner binding (Kamada et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kamada et al., 2017.

claim: BI3802 was reported to possess a poor bioavailability.
source: BI3802 was reported to possess a poor bioavailability (Kerres et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kerres et al., 2017.

claim: FX1 disrupts the interaction between BCL6 and co-repressors with satisfactory antitumor effects in vivo.
source: Therefore, we applied FX1, another BCL6 pharmacological inhibitor, which disrupts the interaction between BCL6 and co-repressors with satisfactory antitumor effects in vivo (Béguelin et al., 2016; Cardenas et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Béguelin et al., 2016; Cardenas et al., 2016.

claim: BCL6 upregulation is a prominent mechanism to protect tumor cells from genotoxic killing.
source: Here, we show that BCL6 upregulation is a prominent mechanism to protect tumor cells from genotoxic killing.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: The transcriptional factor STAT5 serves as a direct negative regulator of BCL6 in lymphomas.
source: It has been reported that the transcriptional factor STAT5 serves as a direct negative regulator of BCL6 in lymphomas (Walker et al., 2007), and FoxO3a promoted BCL6 expression in leukemia cells exposed to BCR-ABL inhibitors (Duy et al., 2011; Fernández de Mattos et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2007.

claim: FoxO3a promoted BCL6 expression in leukemia cells exposed to BCR-ABL inhibitors.
source: It has been reported that the transcriptional factor STAT5 serves as a direct negative regulator of BCL6 in lymphomas (Walker et al., 2007), and FoxO3a promoted BCL6 expression in leukemia cells exposed to BCR-ABL inhibitors (Duy et al., 2011; Fernández de Mattos et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Duy et al., 2011; Fernández de Mattos et al., 2004.

claim: BCL6 could be transactivated by STAT1 in imatinib-treated chronic myeloid leukemia cells.
source: The regulatory mechanism that BCL6 could be transactivated by STAT1 was also observed in imatinib-treated chronic myeloid leukemia cells (Madapura et al., 2017) and contributed to CD4+ T follicular helper cell TFH differentiation and autoimmunity (Nakayamada et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Madapura et al., 2017.

claim: STAT1-mediated BCL6 transactivation contributed to CD4+ T follicular helper cell TFH differentiation and autoimmunity.
source: The regulatory mechanism that BCL6 could be transactivated by STAT1 was also observed in imatinib-treated chronic myeloid leukemia cells (Madapura et al., 2017) and contributed to CD4+ T follicular helper cell TFH differentiation and autoimmunity (Nakayamada et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nakayamada et al., 2014.

claim: The production of cellular mitogenic growth factors and proteases, such as HGF, EGF, and MMP, are programmed during DNA damage to facilitate tumor growth.
source: During DNA damage, the production of cellular mitogenic growth factors and proteases, such as HGF, EGF, and MMP, are programmed to facilitate tumor growth (Bavik et al., 2006; Coppé et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bavik et al., 2006; Coppé et al., 2008.

claim: The production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL6) provoked by chemotherapy will promote anti-apoptotic signaling and intrinsic chemo-resistance.
source: In addition to these pro-survival molecules, the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL6) provoked by chemotherapy, will promote anti-apoptotic signaling and intrinsic chemo-resistance (Gilbert and Hemann, 2010; Hu et al., 2021; Poth et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gilbert and Hemann, 2010; Hu et al., 2021; Poth et al., 2010.

claim: The efficacy of chemotherapeutics is linked to their ability to stimulate a type I interferon response through Toll-like receptor 3.
source: The efficacy of chemotherapeutics is also linked to their ability to stimulate a type I interferon response through Toll-like receptor 3, an intracellular immune receptor that is involved in sensing viruses (Sistigu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sistigu et al., 2014.

claim: The IFN-related DNA damage resistance signature acts as a predictive marker for chemotherapy.
source: These findings support the essential role of IFNs in the tumor microenvironment of conferring drug resistance, along with the fact that the IFN-related DNA damage resistance signature acts as a predictive marker for chemotherapy (Post et al., 2018; Weichselbaum et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Post et al., 2018; Weichselbaum et al., 2008.

claim: Genotoxic therapy-induced damage to the tumor microenvironment promotes treatment resistance through cell nonautonomous effects.
source: Although genotoxic therapy-induced damage to the tumor microenvironment promotes treatment resistance through cell nonautonomous effects (Sun et al., 2012), whether targeting the biologically notable upregulation of IFNs in conjunction with conventional therapy could enhance the treatment response requires additional experimentation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: The BCL6 transcriptional program for the direct silencing of multiple target genes has been elaborated in primary B cells and lymphoma.
source: The BCL6 transcriptional program for the direct silencing of multiple target genes has been elaborated in primary B cells and lymphoma (Ci et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ci et al., 2009.

claim: When acting as a transcriptional repressor, the BCL6 BTB domain recruits the co-repressors NCOR, SMRT, and BCOR.
source: When acting as a transcriptional repressor, the BCL6 BTB domain recruits the co-repressors NCOR, SMRT, and BCOR (Ghetu et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ghetu et al., 2008.

claim: Therapy targeting the BCL6 BTB domain lateral groove displayed inhibitory effects in the treatment of lymphoma.
source: Therapy targeting the BCL6 BTB domain lateral groove displayed inhibitory effects in the treatment of lymphoma (Cheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2018.

claim: BCL6 upregulation is required for maintaining B cells in germinal center compartments.
source: BCL6 upregulation is required for maintaining B cells in germinal center compartments (Choi and Crotty, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Choi and Crotty, 2021.

claim: BCL6 negatively regulates its own transcription by binding to its gene promoter.
source: Once expressed in B cells, BCL6 is tightly controlled through an auto-regulatory circuit model, in which BCL6 negatively regulates its own transcription by binding to its gene promoter (Kikuchi et al., 2000; Pasqualucci et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kikuchi et al., 2000; Pasqualucci et al., 2003.

claim: BRD3 maintained the auto-regulatory circuit of BCL6 by directly interacting with BCL6.
source: We recently reported that BRD3 maintained the auto-regulatory circuit of BCL6 by directly interacting with BCL6 (Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2021.

claim: Aberrant genomic or expressional changes of BCL6 have been detected in lymphomas and multiple solid tumors, including breast cancer, glioblastoma or ovarian cancer.
source: Aberrant genomic or expressional changes of BCL6 have been detected in lymphomas and multiple solid tumors, including breast cancer, glioblastoma or ovarian cancer (Walker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017.

claim: mTOR activation is an actionable mechanism that confers drug resistance.
source: Moreover, the combination of BCL6 inhibitors and genotoxic agents resulted in a marked suppression of the PTEN downstream component mTOR in vivo (Figure 7), reinforcing that mTOR activation is an actionable mechanism that confers drug resistance (Tanaka et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2011.
